result.duty: Tourism Levy Act s.19 (Revised Laws of Saint Lucia 2023) is in force. Registered accommodation providers act as levy collectors and must keep levy funds in a separate account. At the start of the following week they file a weekly report to the SLTA: provider name and registration number, each guest's arrival date and room number, each occupant's name and age, rooms occupied per night, and total guests. Each month, unless the collector agrees otherwise with the SLTA, they file a report with the payment covering guests charged the full levy, guests charged 50%, exempt guests, and totals collected, refunded and remitted. A search summary cites remittance by the 21st of the following month; I did not open that section. The SLTA may audit the books. Collecting the levy without remitting it is fined up to $10,000 for an individual or $100,000 for a company. There is no stated penalty for late reports. Under s.18, failing to disclose the levy when selling online is fined up to $10,000. The rate is US$3 or US$6 per person per night, depending on whether the room rate is below or above US$120. Guests aged 12–17 pay half and under-12s are exempt. These rates come from 2020 sources; I found no change but did not confirm them for 2026.
result.market: I found no official count of the register kept under the SLTA Act. The SLTA's Collection de Pépites marketing programme lists over 400 small accredited properties (B&Bs, inns, villas). A search summary of a May 2026 CHTA article says about 600 short-term rental properties in Saint Lucia are certified. The addressable pool is probably 500–1,000 small providers, which is a small market.
result.reason: The duty is real and in force. Tourism Levy Act (Revised Laws 2023) s.19 requires a weekly guest report and a monthly report with the remittance. One search summary cites a deadline of the 21st of the following month, which I did not confirm. Non-remittance carries fines up to $10k for individuals and $100k for companies. No fine is set for late reports. I found no PMS, app or SLTA online portal for these returns, but I could not open the SLTA website. Its filing channel, which may be an automated system mentioned in 2020, is still unknown. The market is small: the Collection de Pépites programme lists over 400 small properties and CHTA reports about 600 certified short-term rentals. Willingness to pay is likely low. A 7% charge on Airbnb/VRBO stays was announced in 2019–2020 but does not appear in the enacted per-night levy, so I could not tell which applies.

Its scope, whether it covers STRs only or also registration, renewal and sanctions reports, could not be checked because the page only renders a loader. slufia.com has "Supervised Entities (ROSEA)", "Guidelines" and "Downloadable Forms" pages that may hold official templates or guidance; not opened. result.duty: Annual registration with the FIA: Form 1 at first registration (Compliance Manual on AML/CFT/CPF required), then renewal on or before the date on the certificate, with a declaration of compliance and a fee (Act s.7-8). Notices of change in a director, senior manager or beneficial owner, and other material changes, within 14 days (s.13-15). False or misleading information: fine up to $25,000 or 1 year in prison (per the s.16 search summary). Covered categories on Form 1: attorney-at-law, accountant, real estate agent, jeweller, motor vehicle dealer. The Act took effect on 30 March 2023 and the Regulations on 11 April 2023, but the AG Chambers site marks the 2023 text as "not yet authenticated through a Commencement Order". The supervisor is the FIA, which keeps the Register of Supervised Entities (s.12). Not verified: the $300/day penalty, the fee amounts and any transition deadline.
result.market: Not found. The 2021 CFATF MER PDF, which likely has DNFBP sector counts, returned 403. Given Saint Lucia's population of about 180,000, a rough guess is a few hundred covered firms in total (unverified). CFATF's 4th follow-up report (Oct 2024) upgraded R.28 (supervision of DNFBPs) to Largely Compliant, and the 3rd (Jan 2024) upgraded R.22 to LC and R.23 to C. Both point to active supervision.
result.reason: The duty is real. Under the Registration of Supervised Entities Act (Cap. 12.36, in force 30 March 2023) and S.I. 39/2023, attorneys, accountants, real estate agents, jewellers and motor dealers must register with the FIA. Form 1 requires a Compliance Manual, certificates last one year, and renewal needs a declaration of compliance. Changes must be notified within 14 days, and false information carries up to $25,000 or a year in prison. The AG site still labels the text "not yet authenticated". I found no local manual or pack product. However, the FIA runs its own e-filing portal (AMLive Pro), whose scope I couldn't confirm, and has its own ROSEA, guidelines and forms pages. The market is tiny, likely a few hundred firms, and local consultants or accountants probably write these manuals. Low ceiling.

The duty is real: Co-operative Societies Act s.141 requires an annual return within 30 days of the AGM and a monthly return within 30 days of each reporting period, on Registrar forms. It applies to every society, so it covers credit unions. Section 141 states no penalty, and I did not retrieve Part 16. The market is tiny: IMF/FRED lists 16 credit unions and financial cooperatives, with the same figure for 2020-2024, plus some other co-operatives. Competition was not found. Core banking vendors and the League's systems were not identified, and no free portal was found. Whether monthly returns are enforced, and the form format, are unchecked. A market of about 16 buyers and low willingness to pay make a solo-founder business weak.
